content: All collected data should have a clear purpose, and efforts should be made to simplify the processes of recording and reporting. Data on HIV prevention, testing, treatment outcomes, and related infections such as sexually transmitted infections (STIs) and viral hepatitis can be collected through various methods. These include routine data reporting from all patients across healthcare facilities, aggregated data from district health information systems, population-based surveys, case surveillance, cohort observations of people living with HIV, and periodic evaluations. Additionally, program inputs and processes can be monitored through facility surveys, updated service availability lists, documentation of staff availability and training, and tracking the availability of HIV medicines and diagnostics at different levels of the health system using logistics management information systems. Community-based and community-led service data are also critical for effective program monitoring and management. While most routine health information systems are facility-based, data from community-based health services, such as those delivered via mobile or satellite clinics by peer or outreach workers, must also be captured and integrated. Community-led services, often provided by community members to their peers, are particularly important for key populations facing stigma, discrimination, and criminalization, as these individuals may avoid seeking services at conventional health facilities. Community-led services have proven essential in reaching underserved or marginalized populations. These include coordinating data systems of community-led organizations with those of other service providers (e.g. Engaging the community in linking data systems is particularly important for populations that often experience stigma and discrimination in healthcare settings. Strategic linking of unique identifiers (UIDs) for services provided in community-based settings can help avoid double counting of services reported through both community-based and facility-based systems. When collecting key data on HIV programs and responses, it is important to review current monitoring systems, link monitoring of related services (e.g., STIs, tuberculosis, viral hepatitis, and cervical cancer), and include an integrated set of quality-of-care (QoC) indicators relevant for program management. Evaluations or special surveys may be necessary when routine monitoring systems do not provide sufficient or reliable data. Common data sources include routine health information systems, HIV case surveillance systems, laboratory reporting systems, logistics management information systems, health facility assessments, civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems, population-based surveys, special surveys (e.g., drug resistance surveys), and community-led monitoring. Mathematical models can also synthesize routine program data, survey data, and population data to estimate outcomes such as new infections, AIDS-related deaths, and the number of people living with HIV. This data is critical for improving quality-of-care assessments, incorporating community-led monitoring, building linkages between person-centered data and logistics management, and reviewing data from population-based surveys and modeled estimates. Poor-quality care results in more deaths than lack of access to healthcare, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Beyond the loss of life, poor-quality care leads to significant economic losses, exceeding $6 trillion annually. Repeated negative experiences with poor-quality or unsafe care can erode trust in health systems, causing unnecessary human suffering and harm. People living with HIV and those accessing HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and related services deserve high-quality care to achieve and sustain optimal health outcomes and live long, healthy lives. Access to services alone is insufficient if there are gaps in quality of care. Identifying, measuring, and addressing opportunities to improve quality across the care cascade is essential to achieving global targets for ending HIV/AIDS, meeting health-related Sustainable Development Goals, and improving overall health and well-being. Quality must be integrated into all aspects of health systems and service delivery to facilitate effective outcomes and impact for care recipients. Health systems should strive to increase interoperability of tools and systems, such as electronic medical records (EMRs) and patient tracking systems, to enhance accountability and improve care for individuals seeking HIV services. Measuring quality of care requires tracking the delivery of quality health services and promoting accountability. Collecting strategic information at multiple client-provider interfaces and service delivery points provides visibility into services that can be addressed through quality improvement initiatives. Person-centered care emphasizes integrated care for HIV and related infections across the life course. Mechanisms to share findings and adapt services based on data and implementation experience are key. While routine data should be the primary source, additional approaches may be warranted to gather data on patient experiences and satisfaction not captured through routine programmatic data. Qualitative methods, such as surveys and focus group discussions, can provide valuable insights into patient and healthcare worker experiences. Validated tools and resources, such as those from the Institute for Healthcare Improvement and WHO, can support quality improvement efforts. Priority populations for measuring quality of care include children, adolescents, pregnant and breastfeeding women, key populations (e.g., men who have sex with men, sex workers, transgender individuals, people who inject drugs, and incarcerated individuals), individuals with advanced HIV, and older adults living with HIV. For example, mental health conditions, HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders, and palliative care are critical components of comprehensive care for people living with HIV and should be considered when measuring quality of care. Community engagement plays a vital role in measuring quality of care and holding stakeholders accountable for providing high-quality services. Community-led organizations and stakeholders, particularly those representing specific subgroups, offer invaluable insights into service quality and gaps that quantitative data may not capture. Improving and sustaining quality of care requires planning, commitment, and sufficient resources from policymakers. Programs should strive to enhance quality at all stages of the HIV care cascade, from prevention to end-of-life care.
